title: Timing programs and tempos on the Streckfus excursion boats
summary: The company timed each program so many numbers fit, with leaders keeping precise tempos and faster Lindy hop tempos required in St. Louis.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable

blocks.x: Now they were, like Captain Brown that I know played the violin, and some of them, like Captain Joe, I learned to play the piano. And they really knew me. They knew how, I tell you what I would know is they were good at, you see, making your program on that boat. Your music had to be timed to get a certain many numbers within the program. The program ran from about four, and they always had what they call side numbers, you see, and you always had to have numbers, you had to time yourself, a certain program, and the program ran from about one to fourteen. Then you had two parts of that program, or three parts of it where you played a waltz set, you see. And that music had to be timed so that you had to get so many numbers within a program. And they had that time of timing music by watching a watch. They could tell you just what tempo, because fate, that was one thing a leader had to be very precise in the knocking off a tempo if it was supposed to be forty or fifty or sixty, like that, metronome beats, you know. You had to be very careful about that. And they had numbers that they didn't want you to play too fast and not too slow. And down in Yaw Range there was a certain way you had to play when you got to St. Louis. There was a different way. In St. Louis you had to play a more fast tune, because they were dancing that Lindy Hoppin thing back in that time. And that's why I actually hadn't had the experience of playing the fastest tempo I ever played playing music, especially when we got to St. Louis. So getting on back to you, so when I came back here ...
